questions.prompt: A substance has a urine concentration of 100 mg/dL and a plasma concentration of 1 mg/dL, and urine flow is 1 mL/min. What is its clearance?
questions.explanation: Clearance = (U × V) ÷ P = (100 mg/dL × 1 mL/min) ÷ 1 mg/dL = 100 mL/min: 100 mL of plasma is cleared of the substance each minute.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate renal clearance from urine and plasma concentrations and urine flow.

questions.prompt: A 74-year-old on lisinopril takes ibuprofen for a week of back pain during a bout of diarrhea. Her creatinine doubles. What is the mechanism?

choices.a: Afferent constriction (prostaglandins blocked) plus efferent dilation (angiotensin II blocked) lowers glomerular pressure.
choices.b: Ibuprofen directly poisons the collecting duct.

questions.explanation: With volume depletion, glomerular filtration depends on prostaglandins dilating the afferent arteriole and angiotensin II constricting the efferent. NSAIDs remove the first and ACE inhibitors the second, so glomerular pressure and GFR fall: prerenal acute kidney injury.
questions.learning_objective: Explain acute kidney injury from NSAIDs with ACE inhibitors in volume depletion.

questions.prompt: Why do people with poorly controlled diabetes have glucose in their urine?

choices.a: Insulin normally pumps glucose back from urine.
choices.b: Filtered glucose exceeds the proximal tubule's SGLT capacity, so the rest is excreted.

questions.explanation: Glucose is freely filtered and normally all reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by SGLT2 (and SGLT1). Above a plasma glucose of roughly 180–200 mg/dL, the transporters saturate and glucose appears in the urine. SGLT2 inhibitors exploit this.
questions.learning_objective: Explain glucosuria in terms of proximal tubular transport maximum.

questions.prompt: Furosemide acts by inhibiting which transporter, in which segment?

choices.b: NCC, in the distal convoluted tubule
choices.c: NKCC2, in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

questions.explanation: Loop diuretics block the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2) of the thick ascending limb, which reabsorbs about a quarter of filtered sodium, so they are the most potent diuretics. Side effects include hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia and ototoxicity.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the site and transporter targeted by loop diuretics.

questions.prompt: A patient with heart failure takes lisinopril and is started on spironolactone. Which lab value most needs watching?
questions.explanation: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone in the collecting duct, reducing K⁺ secretion; ACE inhibitors lower aldosterone too. Together they can cause dangerous hyperkalemia, especially with kidney impairment.
questions.learning_objective: Anticipate hyperkalemia with spironolactone and ACE inhibitors.

questions.prompt: A patient with small-cell lung cancer has a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L, is not dehydrated, and has concentrated urine. What best explains this?

choices.a: Inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH): water is retained through aquaporin-2

questions.explanation: SIADH (here from the tumor) keeps aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct, so water is retained and sodium diluted despite a normal volume, with inappropriately concentrated urine. Diabetes insipidus gives dilute urine and high or normal sodium.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize SIADH and explain it through ADH action in the collecting duct.
